newsitem.title: USA: Evergreen Media merging with Chancellor. [CORRECTED 01:00 GMT 19/2]
newsitem.headline: Evergreen Media merging with Chancellor. [CORRECTED 01:00 GMT 19/2]

text.p: Evergreen Media Corp., the nation's largest radio broadcasting company, moved Tuesday to bolster its position with an agreement to merge with Chancellor Broadcasting Co. and acquire 10 radio properties owned by Viacom Inc.
The merger and the $1.075 billion purchase of the Viacom stations will create a business worth $5 billion, the companies said.
"This takes them from three companies with pretty strong positions to a juggernaut," said Bankers Trust analyst Mark McFadden.
The 10 Viacom properties are in Los Angeles, Chicago, New York, Washington and Detroit.
The combined Evergreen and Chancellor, to be called Chancellor Media Corp., will have 103 radio stations in 21 U.S. markets, with 1996 net revenues of more than $700 million, Evergreen said.

Even before the deal, Evergreen was the nation's largest radio broadcasting company, with 42 major-market stations in 11 markets. While Evergreen has focused on being a player in the top 10 markets, Chancellor focused on stations in the top 50 markets.
Although Evergreen and Chancellor had each made independent plays for Viacom's stations, the decision to join forces minimises the financial impact, analysts said.
"If either separately chose to pay this price for Viacom, there would've been a significant dilutive effect on their stock," UBS Securities analyst Edward Hatch said.
"It would've been a very big pill to swallow," added Oppenheimer & Co. analyst Edward Atorino.

Evergreen Chairman Scott Ginsburg said in a conference call with reporters that the company expects to swap or sell at least eight stations: two FM stations in San Francisco, two FM stations in Chicago, one FM station in Detroit, an FM and two AM stations in Washington, D.C.

The deal is viewed as a direct result of last year's passage of the Telecommunications Act, which loosened restrictions on ownership of radio stations in any single market, and has led to a spate of consolidations among broadcasting companies. As a result, companies such as Evergreen and Chancellor were forced to consider such moves now, while there are enough competitors to gobble up.
There are some 11,000 radio stations in the country.

Until the Telecommunications Act was enacted, companies were limited to owning no more than four radio statons in any one large market. Companies may now own eight radio stations in each large market.
The new law also places no overall cap on total ownership nationwide. Previously, companies could own no more than 40.
"There's a once-in-a-lifetime chance," Bankers Trust's McFadden said. "You either do it now, or the door shuts forever. ... In about two years, there won't be any. So you have to buy them now."

Under the deal, Evergreen will give Chancellor about $600 million in stock and assume about $900 million in debt. (Corrects common stock value from $568 miilion to $600 million and correts debt value from about $922 million to about $900 million.)
Evergreen said it would swap 0.9091 share of its Class A common stock for each share of Chancellor.

After the merger, which is expected to be tax-free, Evergreen stockholders will hold two-thirds of the combined companies' roughly 63 million common shares, while Chancellor shareholders will hold one-third, Evergreen said.
Chancellor Broadcasting Chairman Thomas Hicks will be chairman of Chancellor Media Corp.
Evergreen Chairman and Chief Executive Scott Ginsburg will be the new company's president and chief executive, and Evergreen Chief Financial Officer Matthew Devine will be the new company's CFO.
The Evergreen-Chancellor merger agreement requires regulatory approval and approval by shareholders of both companies, Evergreen said.
Chancellor's stock gained 6.25 cents to close at $28 while Evergreen lost $1.25 to $31.50, both on the Nasdaq market.
